cards.front: Define the curl of a 3D vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle$ using the $\nabla$ operator.
cards.back:
The curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is defined as $\text{curl } \mathbf{F} = \nabla \times \mathbf{F}$, which can be computed as the determinant:
$$\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ P & Q & R \end{vmatrix}$$

cards.front: What physical property of a vector field does the curl vector quantify?
cards.back: The curl quantifies the "rotation" or "swirliness" of a vector field at a given point. More precisely, it measures the maximum circulation per unit area at that point.

cards.front: Write out the component form of $\text{curl } \mathbf{F} = \nabla \times \mathbf{F}$ for $\mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle$.
cards.back:
The component form is:
$$\text{curl } \mathbf{F} = \left( \frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z} \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( \frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial R}{\partial x} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right)\mathbf{k}$$

cards.front: Calculate $\text{curl } \mathbf{F}$ for the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \langle yz, xz, xy \rangle$.
cards.back:
Given $\mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle = \langle yz, xz, xy \rangle$. We compute the partial derivatives:
$\frac{\partial R}{\partial y} = x$, $\frac{\partial Q}{\partial z} = x \implies \frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z} = x-x=0$
$\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} = y$, $\frac{\partial R}{\partial x} = y \implies \frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial R}{\partial x} = y-y=0$
$\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = z$, $\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = z \implies \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = z-z=0$
Thus, $\text{curl } \mathbf{F} = \langle 0,0,0 \rangle = \mathbf{0}$.

cards.front: How does the direction of the curl vector $\text{curl } \mathbf{F}$ relate to the axis of rotation of the fluid?
cards.back: The direction of the curl vector indicates the axis about which the rotation (or circulation) of the fluid is greatest at that point. Its direction is determined by the right-hand rule: if you curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of the rotation, your thumb points in the direction of the curl vector.

cards.front: What does it mean for a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ to be "irrotational," and what is its mathematical condition?
cards.back: A vector field $\mathbf{F}$ is "irrotational" if its curl is the zero vector everywhere, i.e., $\text{curl } \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}$. In simply connected domains, an irrotational vector field is also a conservative field, meaning it can be expressed as the gradient of some scalar potential function, $\mathbf{F} = \nabla f$.

cards.front: State Stokes' Theorem and explain how it connects the curl to circulation.
cards.back: Stokes' Theorem states: $\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\text{curl } \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S}$. It relates the circulation of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ around a closed curve $C$ to the flux of the curl of $\mathbf{F}$ through any surface $S$ bounded by $C$. This means the curl can be interpreted as the "circulation density" or "infinitesimal circulation per unit area" at a point.

cards.front: The magnitude of $\text{curl } \mathbf{F}$ at a point represents what specific property related to rotation?
cards.back: The magnitude $|\text{curl } \mathbf{F}|$ at a point represents the maximum circulation per unit area (or maximum angular speed) at that point. The direction of the vector $\text{curl } \mathbf{F}$ indicates the axis of this maximum rotation.
